zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent reading: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The supplied subset aided entry identification and coverage; this review’s readings and English notes are independent and remain controlled by the supplied BnF scan.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page with an explanation involving oral instruction: teaching by word of mouth. The opening fragment remains separate; its missing beginning is not supplied.
Mooshitsuzuke means continuing a discourse, directly matching continuar a pratica. The historical principal parts and the printed open long-o mark are retained.
Mooshitodome means stopping or detaining someone by speaking. The Portuguese object alguem is followed by the means on the next row.
Palauras completes com palauras: the person is detained with words. This short continuation is a complete physical row, not another entry.
Mooshitogame is verbal reproach or rebuke. The headword has a downward long-o mark in this impression, correcting the draft circumflex rather than normalizing the spelling.
Com palauras across the two rows specifies that the reproach is spoken. The same short gloss ending above belongs to a different verb and is not a duplicated row.
Mooshitotonoye means arranging or settling something through discussion. The scan reads the single Portuguese word algum, not the draft al zum.
Negocio com falar completes the description of settling an affair by talking. The historical negocio is retained without adding a modern accent.
Mooshitoonoki describes withdrawing from another person's conversation. The Portuguese pratica is physically divided after pra-, with a visible terminal hyphen.
Tica completes pratica, followed by the synonymous conuersação de outro. Both glosses concern another person's discourse, not physical distance alone.
Mooshitoori means proceeding through what one says or telling it through to the end. The printed ru, otta principal parts belong to the Japanese verb.
Dizer atè o cabo completes the alternative gloss: saying something all the way to its conclusion. The final accent is preserved as printed.
Mooshiwake denotes explaining or defending oneself, hence dar rezão em defensa. Preserve the printed quru principal part rather than replacing it with an expected modern conjugation.
Mooshiwatashi means giving an oral charge or instruction. The damaged medial letter is read as t, supported by its surviving stem and the bilingual context, rather than the draft r.
Sa completes couſa; de palaura specifies that the charge is given orally. No new headword begins on this continuation.

runs.text: Sal que ſe faz acendendo o forno cõ

lines.note: Moshio is salt produced with dried marine plants as fuel. The definition begins with heating the furnace and continues with the kind of fuel below; it is distinct from the surrounding mooshi- verbs.

runs.text: certas eruas, ou limos do mar ſecos. Vt,

lines.note: The fuel consists of dried sea plants or seaweed. Vt introduces moshio wo yaku, with the initial Mo- on this row and the rest below.
Moshio wo yaku is rendered as making salt by burning those plants. The object-particle sequence xiuouo belongs to the divided example, not to a new entry.
Limos secos completes the dried-seaweed gloss. The final upright S. is the written-language label and is not italic Portuguese prose.

Mooshiokure denotes failing to make a due courteous communication in time. The Portuguese begins a description of omitted social courtesies; de- continues into deuidos below. The worn long-o mark does not securely distinguish its direction; the baseline circumflex in Môxivocure is retained.

runs.text: uidos comprimentos por paßar o tempo deuido,

lines.note: The due courtesies are missed because their proper time has passed. The scan has the continuous word comprimentos, preserving the historical spelling rather than the draft's internal space.

runs.text: ou conueniente, em q̃ os ouuera de fazer.

lines.note: Completes the timing condition: the suitable occasion on which the courtesies should have been performed. The abbreviation q̃ is retained without expansion.
Mooshiokuri means sending word or having a message conveyed. The short Portuguese mandar dizer supplies the causative communication sense.
Moshiogusa is glossed as a book of history or poetry. Its final upright P. is the poetry label, not part of the italic definition.
Mooshioki means leaving something said or stated for later reference. Deixar dito distinguishes it from the preceding act of sending word.

Mooshiosame means finishing one's speech. The surviving o and voſame, with the Portuguese gloss and the supplied NINJAL lexical aid, support Moxivoſame rather than Mixicoſame. No long-o mark is secure at the abraded opening, so none is supplied.
Mooshiotoshi means omitting something in speech. The following Portuguese row supplies the reason for the omission: forgetfulness.
Esquecimento completes por esquecimento, specifying accidental omission rather than deliberate refusal to speak.
Mooshiuke is receiving something deferentially from a noble person. The printed v before qe supplies the u of uke; the draft had omitted that letter.
Peßoa nobre completes the source of the respectfully received thing. This row belongs to mooshiuke and retains the historical double-s sort.

Mooshiuketamawari is glossed as hearing and speaking between people. The printed sequence is xivqe-, not the draft xioq-. The long-o mark is reduced to an oblique remnant; the draft circumflex is retained as a nonblocking graphic uncertainty.
Lar completes falar after fa-; entre si gives the reciprocal setting of the hearing and speaking. This gloss should not be silently replaced by a narrower modern sense.
Mooshishizume means calming or pacifying someone through words. The headword is continuous despite abrasion; the draft's space after Mǒ did not mark a word boundary.
Ziguar completes apa-ziguar, a second verb for pacifying. The small internal letters are worn but their surviving traces support ziguar rather than the draft zguar.
Mooshiyaburi means undoing or refuting another person's statement. The printed Portuguese desfazer introduces the verbal means on this and the following row.
Uras completes palauras, followed by o que outro diz: what another person says. The two rows form one definition of verbal refutation.
Mooshuu is explained by midari no shuujaku, disordered attachment. The Portuguese begins an account of being engrossed in or attached to sin; the punctuation after metido is a comma.

runs.text: ou afeiçoado a peccado, preſo de ſuas paixõ-

lines.note: The attachment is described as affection for sin and captivity to one's passions. Paixõ- is visibly divided before es on the next row.
Es completes paixões and the abbreviation &c. closes the explanation. This is the end of the attachment sense, not the beginning of the following homograph.
The next mooshuu is equated with shichigatsu, the seventh lunar month. The scan reads Septima with a t, correcting the draft Sepima.

Mooshun, explained as hajime no haru, means the beginning of spring. Principio corrects draft Principia. The worn long-o mark retains the draft circumflex; the lexical identification does not settle its original direction.
Mauera completes primauera, closing the early-spring gloss. The apparent modern spelling primavera is not imposed on the source.

runs.text: Moxxu. i, Fitono atouo qexxo ſuru.

lines.note: Mosshu is paraphrased as confiscating another person's estate. Qexxo suru belongs to the Japanese explanation after i, and is not an embedded Portuguese term.
Fiscar completes con-fiscar; os bens dalguem explicitly identifies the property being confiscated. The whole gloss belongs to mosshu.
Moyai is glossed by tsunagiawasuru, joining or tying together. The Portuguese Da- begins darem and introduces the practical example of linking boats.

runs.text: rem os cabos hũas Funes as outras pera ſe pode-

lines.note: The boats pass cables to one another so people can communicate and cross between them. Funes is the Japanese boat term embedded, with Portuguese plural marking, in an otherwise Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: rem cõmunicar, & paßar de hũa Fune à outra.

lines.note: Rem completes poderem. The scan reads cõmunicar as one word, followed by passage from one Fune to another; Fune is an embedded Japanese boat term. A very faint trace at the baseline after outra is adopted as a terminal period; its weakness remains a nonblocking punctuation uncertainty.

runs.text: O liar, ou amarrar hũa embarcação à

lines.note: Moyai here is the nominal act of tying or mooring one vessel to another. The final preposition leads directly into outra on the next physical row.
Outra completes the mooring definition. Moyai wo toru is the accompanying example of taking or making the mooring connection.
Moya is a damp, rainy mist. The scan reads chuuoſa, retaining historical u for consonantal v; the draft inserted an extra n.
Moya ga orita says that the mist came down. The Portuguese gives the parallel verbs cahio and abaixouſe, with eſ-ta divided below.
Ta neuoa completes esta neuoa, the mist referred to in the Japanese example. The short row closes the entry.
Moyashi here is the transitive act of making seed germinate. Fazer nacer and arrebentar are the two Portuguese descriptions of sprouting.

runs.text: a ſemente de trigo, grãos, ou outros legumes

lines.note: The seed is wheat, pulses, or other legumes. Semente is one printed word; the draft's se mente was an artificial split.
The seeds are put in water and then covered or kept close. These preparation steps explain the preceding sprouting sense, not the burning sense below.
The noun moyashi is illustrated by mugi or mame no moyashi, wheat or bean sprouts. The example's final word is divided after moya-.

runs.text: Olhos, ou gomos do trigo, ou grãos que

lines.note: Xi completes moyashi. Olhos and gomos identify the shoots or buds produced by the grain or pulses.
Arrebentam desta maneira refers back to the germination method just described. The print's provisional st allograph is retained pending the specialist typography pass.
A distinct moyashi entry means causing something to burn. Hi wo begins the fire-lighting example on the same row.
Moyasu completes hi wo moyasu, rendered as lighting the fire. This causative action contrasts with the intransitive moye in the next entry.
Moye is the intransitive verb: the fire burns. The principal parts uru and eta are preserved in their historical form.
Moyeagari means flames rising high. The Portuguese reads grande, not gronde; the subject labareda follows on the next row.
The example begins yacata ni hi wo kaketareba, setting fire to a residence or building. The following rows describe the resulting flames and smoke.
The flames rise vigorously and black smoke follows. The long-vowel spelling miǒyen is retained from the visible text, without substituting a normalized Japanese transcription.
Ten wo kasumetari completes the smoke darkening the sky. Taif. is the upright citation label; Lib. 70. is retained as visibly printed, rather than changing the number to fit an assumed source.

runs.text: Pondo fogo nas caſas, & aleuantandoſe grãde

lines.note: The Portuguese translation repeats setting fire to houses and the rising of a great flame. The abbreviation grãde preserves its nasal mark.

runs.text: labareda a fumaça eſcurecia ao ceo.

lines.note: The smoke darkened the sky, completing the quoted fire scene. The historical ceo is retained rather than modern céu.

runs.text: Tição, ou pao que fica queimado a-

lines.note: Moyekui is a charred stick or firebrand, even when it no longer burns. The final a- begins ainda on the next row.
The definition explicitly allows a firebrand without live fire. Moyekui ni hi ga begins an example about how easily it catches again.

runs.text: No pao queimado, ou tição fa-

lines.note: Tsukiyoi completes the claim that fire readily catches on a previously burnt stick. The Portuguese facilmente is divided after fa-.

runs.text: cilmente ſe pega o fogo. ¶ Item, per met.

lines.note: Cilmente completes facilmente; the fire catches easily. Item, per met. introduces the figurative application that follows.

runs.text: Eſtar facilitado pera cair ẽ peccado por via da

lines.note: The figurative sense is susceptibility to falling into sin. This is the dictionary's moral comparison, not a literal second description of wood.
The prior occasion of sin remains nearby, explaining the susceptibility. The printed estar is retained with the draft's provisional st treatment.
Moyekusa is glossed by the historical Portuguese disease-name Eriſipula. This entry is not the plant-germination sense suggested by the preceding moye- forms.
Moyegi is defined here as dark green. The dictionary's stated shade is retained without substituting a modern colour standard.
Mooyei is equated with fude, a writing implement. The scan has a clear circumflex on o and an upright final S. usage label.
Moyeide in this entry means plants beginning to sprout. The printed zzuru principal part belongs to the historical idzuru form, not a doubled-letter OCR error.
Herbs, wheat, and similar plants are the subjects that begin to grow. This short continuation closes the germination sense.
The next moyeide concerns flames beginning to rise. Its identical headword is intentionally repeated for the burning sense.

runs.text: a labareda, ou acenderſe o fogo.

lines.note: The flame rises or the fire catches. The scan reads acenderſe, with c rather than the draft r in arenderſe.
Moyesashi is a firebrand or partly burnt piece of wood. It is a separate synonym, not an inflected continuation of moyeide.
Moyesusari has the same meaning as the preceding firebrand term. The upright B. marks low or vulgar usage and remains outside the italic Idem.
Moyetsuki means fire taking hold or catching. The scan has a continuous headword and the continuous Portuguese verb Atearſe, correcting both artificial spaces in the draft.
Pegarſe completes the alternative expression for fire catching. This brief row closes the entry before the noun moyoo.
Moyoo denotes manner, gesture, or bodily movements here. The gloss is broader than a modern textile-pattern sense and is left as the source states it.
Moyooshi means arousing, prompting, or moving someone. The examples that follow distinguish religious fervour from assembling people for war.
Shinjin wo moyoosu means stirring up religious devotion. The Portuguese excitarſe is followed by a further expression for becoming inflamed with devotion.
The scan reads acenderſe em deuação, lighting up with devotion, rather than the draft atenderſe. Ninju wo moyoosu then begins the example of mobilizing people.

runs.text: Excitar, & aparelhar a gente pera a

lines.note: Uoſu completes moyoosu. The Portuguese describes rousing and preparing people for a purpose supplied below.
Guerra completes the mobilization example: preparing people for war. The continuation is not a separate military headword.
The noun moyooshi is fervour or preparation for something. The worn middle letter of Fervor is read as v, not the draft t; the gloss matches the preceding examples.

runs.text: Eſpecies, ou fantaſmas que ſe repreſẽ-

lines.note: Moozoo concerns images or phantasms of improper things. Both o marks point downward in this impression; the first is not the draft circumflex.

runs.text: tão de couſas torpes, ou deſordenadas. ¶ Per

lines.note: The images concern shameful or disordered things. Deſordenadas is the adopted reading of a heavily abraded span: surviving o/r/d traces and the Portuguese context support it, but several strokes remain weak.
Per met. introduces moozoo wo miru, seeing such things in dreams. The Portuguese object continues in torpes on the bottom body row, which the draft had merged with the catchword.
Torpes completes the improper things seen in dreams. This left-positioned italic word is running text, not the catchword; the separately placed Mozu. anticipates the next page’s bird entry.
